2. The facts relevant for disposal of the Rule are that the plaintiff-petitioners instituted Title Suit No. 63 of 1999 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Thana Shyamnagar, Satkhira against the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 to 4 for declaration of title and enlistment of the suit land as vested property is illegal, collusive, ultra vires, fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiffs. The plaintiff-petitioners alleged, inter alia, that the suit land appertaining to SA Khatian No. 393 of Mouza Gabura, Police Station Shyamnagar area measuring 6.81½ decimals originally belonged to one Fazu Sarder and other co-sharer and out of that 4.37 acres of land is subject matter of the suit as described in "Ka" schedule of the plaint That Fazu Sarder died living behind 4 sons namely, Omar Ali Sarder, Gahar Ali, Sahar Ali and Anser Ali. The said successors and other co-sharer from 1966 onwards transferred their lands part by part to the predecessor of the plaintiffs and also plaintiff-petitioners vide different deeds of sale and by means of such transfer, the plaintiff-petitioners became the owners of the suit land and continued to enjoy the suit land by way of cultivation and residing in dwelling houses in some portion of the suit land by paying rents to the government for a long period but in spite of this the local Tahsildar, defendant No.4, threatened the plaintiffs on 10-6-1999 to disturb the peaceful possession of the suit land by giving Ejara of the suit land to the 3rd party treating as vested property and hence, the suit. 

 8. Mr AY Ahmed Ali, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that the learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in reversing order of temporary injunction of the trial Court without setting aside the material findings recorded by the learned Assistant Judge with reference to the deeds of sale and on assigning cogent reasons and the same has occasioned failure of justice. Mr Ahmed Ali further submits that the learned Court of Appeal below also ignored the material findings of the trial Court in respect of the documents filed by the plaintiffs, such as SA Khatian, 14 registered kabala deeds, yearly rent receipts, recent survey khatians and the plaintiffs' peaceful possession in the suit property and, as such, the impugned judgment of the lower Appellate Court is liable to be set aside. He finally, submits that admittedly the petitioners are in possession of the suit properties for over 25 years, since their purchase from the date of their vendors and they have been enjoying and possessing the same by payments of rents to the Government and, in such, situation the defendant Government could not dispossess them and on these consideration the trial Court rightly allowed the prayer for temporary injunction but the learned Court of Appeal below failed to apply his judicial mind in appreciating the plaintiff-petitioner's case from a correct angle and fell into error in deciding the prima facie case and balance of convenience and inconvenience of the parties and, as such, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. 

 11. It appears from the order passed by the trial Court that after hearing the parties the trial Court found that the plaintiff-petitioners had a prima facie good arguable case on the ground that the plaintiffs filed a number of registered deeds, khatians, dakhilas and tax receipts, etc in respect of the suit land and which are important items of evidence of possession and thereby the learned Assistant Judge came to a finding that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land on the strength of documents, such as registered deeds, khatians, dakhilas and tax receipts, etc. The trial Court also found that the Government defendant could not or did not file any document that one Narayan Chandra purchased 3.32 acres of suit land from CS recorded tenants and who left this country for India in 1965 and thereon the suit land was enlisted as vested property. 

 15. For the reasons stated above, I hold that the plaintiffs-petitioners have been able to establish a good prima facie arguable case inasmuch as they have filed a number of documents and papers in support of their claim, such as 14 registered deeds, khatians, dakhilas and tax receipts, etc and thus, therefore, the well-established principles of law governing the grant of temporary injunction are 1) the plaintiff has to establish a good prima facie case 2) it has to be shown that the plaintiff will suffer irreparable loss, if the injunction prayed for is not granted and 3) the balance of convenience and inconvenience lies in favour of the plaintiff and in favour of granting the temporary injunction prayed for, are attracted in its entirety in this case. Therefore, on that score the learned subordinate judge erred in law in reversing the order of temporary injunction passed by the learned trial Court and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. However, here it may be mentioned that Mr AY Ahmed Ali, the Advocate, at the end of the day frankly submits that he will have no objection, if the order of temporary injunction be modified by substituting it with an order for maintaining status quo pending disposal of the suit which will also serve the interest of the plaintiff-petitioners.
